issues.legal_issue: A statutory requirement to deposit part of a demand before a revision against an adjudicated demand is entertained is a valid condition on the statutory right of revision.
material_facts: The initial authority determined the value of the property and demanded additional stamp duty, registration charges, and a penalty.
The applicable law required proof of payment of fifty percent of the recoverable amount before a revision against that determination could be entertained.
The required payment applied at the revisional stage, after the initial adjudication of the demand.
issues.conclusion: The deposit requirement was constitutionally valid and did not render the right of revision illusory.
issues.legal_principle: A right of appeal or revision created by statute is not an absolute right; the legislature may impose conditions on its exercise. The Court applied Section 65(1) of the Rajasthan Stamp Act, 1998, and its proviso, and Article 14 of the Constitution. Relying on Government of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Laxmi Devi, The Anant Mills Co. Ltd. v. State of Gujarat, Vijay Prakash D. Mehta v. Collector of Customs (Preventive), and Gujarat Agro Industries Co. Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Ahmedabad, the Court held that the deposit condition was a permissible condition on revision. It distinguished Mardia Chemical Ltd. v. Union of India because the deposit there was required before the first adjudication, whereas this requirement operated after the initial adjudication.

predicates.revision_challenges_first_adjudication: A person seeks revision of a demand that has already been determined by an initial adjudicatory authority.
predicates.partial_deposit_is_revisional_condition: The governing process requires the person to pay part of the recoverable demand before the revision can be entertained.
predicates.deposit_applies_after_initial_adjudicati: The required payment is imposed at the revision stage, after the initial adjudication of the demand.

issues.definition: When a revision challenges an already-adjudicated demand and payment of part of that demand is a condition at the revision stage, that condition is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: A court may not reject a writ challenging a property valuation and resulting demand solely because a revision is available when that revision requires a partial deposit, without examining whether the demand is alleged to be so exorbitant that the revision remedy is ineffective.
material_facts: The property owner challenged the valuation and resulting demand by writ petition.
A revision was available, but it could not be entertained without proof of payment of fifty percent of the recoverable amount.
The property owner alleged that the valuation and demand were exorbitant.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the basis of the alternative revision remedy without examining whether the valuation and demand were exorbitant.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the High Court orders and remanded the writ petition for fresh consideration, including examination of whether the valuation and demand were exorbitant so as to make revision ineffective.
issues.legal_principle: Although an alternative statutory remedy may ordinarily be relevant to whether a writ petition is entertained, a party is not remediless where a demand is alleged to be arbitrary or exorbitant. Under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court should examine whether the valuation and demand are exorbitant and whether the deposit requirement makes revision ineffective. The Court applied Government of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Laxmi Devi, including its reliance on Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India for the principle that arbitrariness violates Article 14.

predicates.writ_challenges_property_valuation_deman: A person brings a writ petition challenging a determination of property value and the resulting demand.
predicates.alternative_revision_requires_partial_de: The available revision cannot be entertained unless the person first pays part of the demanded amount.
predicates.exorbitance_is_alleged: The person alleges that the valuation or resulting demand is exorbitant or arbitrary.
predicates.high_court_dismisses_without_assessing_e: The High Court rejects the writ petition because a revision is available without assessing whether the valuation or demand is exorbitant.

issues.definition: When a writ challenges a property valuation and resulting demand, revision requires partial payment, and exorbitance is alleged but not assessed, the High Court must reconsider whether the demand makes revision ineffective.
